rationale: A wins because it keeps the four stories cleaner: money, moat, driver, connector standard, each with a real beat and a real proof burden. Its best line, 'An unprofitable automaker just turned its charging network into a revenue line,' is a business story an editor can understand in three seconds. B is strong, but 'Every new Rivian stall will carry both plugs — the connector fight is over' overclaims the supplied facts and drags a good standards angle into pundit fog.
gaps_in_A: 'The prevailing belief: a proprietary fast-charging network is a moat' is plausible but not in the provided update; it needs outside evidence before it can anchor the contrarian angle.
'what it says about the moat thesis the rest of the industry still holds' overreaches from one Rivian access change to an industry-wide belief.
'Rivian follows Tesla's Supercharger playbook' is refused for being unsupported, but the refusal is slightly over-lawyered; outside context could make that comparison valid if sourced.
gaps_in_B: 'the connector fight is over' is headline malpractice. The facts say Rivian will put CCS and NACS on new stalls; they do not settle an industry standards fight.
'joining the small set of automaker-owned networks that sell to non-owners' is an unsourced market claim not present in the update.
'operators eating the hardware cost of supporting both standards through a long overlap' invents cost structure and transition economics the update does not give.
'competing for the same drivers rather than negotiating with their manufacturers' turns 'no partnership announced' into a strategic posture. That is how corrections are born.
